Business.title: Stung by Trump, machinists union campaigns for affordability in midterms
Business.text:
The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM), one of the largest labor unions in the US, has launched a “workers v billionaires” political campaign tour targeting members in eight battleground states and encouraging them to support pro-worker candidates in the midterms.

IAM has nearly 700,000 active and retired members in North America, covering workers at corporations that include Boeing, Lockheed Martin, United Airlines and Harley-Davidson. The union is targeting members and voters in Maine, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Arizona, Nevada and Illinois.

“We made a strategic commitment that we’re going to be the most engaged that we have ever been in the history of our union in working,” said Brian Bryant, international president of IAM. “We’re living in an economy that only favors billionaires and does not favor working people, and it’s time that Congress and this administration realize who they should be looking out for.”

Bryant emphasized that several union members, including those with IAM, voted for Trump in 2024 because of promises that he would fix the economy and make things more affordable. Throughout his 2024 presidential campaign, Trump repeatedly claimed: “When I win, I will immediately bring prices down, starting on day one.”

Yet since Trump took office, inflation has increased from 3.0% in January 2025 to 3.4% in August 2026, health insurance costs are soaring due to the expiration of Affordable Care Act subsidies and gas prices are on average $1 a gallon higher due to Trump’s war with Iran.

The union will “send a message to this administration that what the status quo is right now is not acceptable, and they’re going to have to stand up and pay attention to working people”, Bryant said.

Jason Gayler, president of IAM local 776A in Fort Worth, Texas, said his state “is more purple than what people put out to be”. As Democrats are seeking to flip several seats, polls are showing that races are the most competitive they’ve been in decades.

“The price of just the cost of living in north Texas now has absolutely skyrocketed, and it’s starting to really affect a lot of our members, which is motivating them to back candidates that focus primarily on the working class,” Gayler said.

He also noted that the machinists recently elected their first rank-and-file member to the Texas senate; Taylor Rehmet, president of the IAM’s Texas state council, won a special election in January, flipping a state senate district that Trump won in 2024 by 17%.

Shay Blodgett, an Alaska Airlines worker in Phoenix who is helping to lead IAM’s political program in Arizona, said the union has worked to oppose Republican-led state legislation that would have restricted public sector workers’ ability to organize and supported the Arizona AFL-CIO “labor 2026 blitz” campaign.

“We’ve been conducting member-to-member engagement this summer, reaching out, asking members what matters to them,” Blodgett said. “We heard them loud and clear. The No 1 thing was the economy, cost of living, fuel prices, healthcare and food costs.”

Co-workers have expressed regret over voting for Republicans in the last election, especially since transportation workers are exempt from the temporary no-tax-on-overtime deduction that was passed as part of Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act that was passed last summer.

“The majority of our airline workers in the state will be entering contract negotiations in early 2027, and we need elected officials that will fix the economy and allow airline workers to fulfill the American dream of home ownership and raising families in Arizona,” Blodgett said.

Rich Howell, former president of IAM local 1776, a longtime member of the union and worker at Philadelphia international airport, said the union is supporting Democrats in Pennsylvania who are trying to flip four congressional districts and the state senate while maintaining control of the governorship and statehouse.

Trump “said he was going to bring down the prices a year and a half ago. That was his campaign message. If you go back and see all the promises, there wasn’t one that he held,” Howell said.

He noted this is a difficult election year due to the amount of money billionaires are pouring into politics – more than $1.6bn in the 2026 midterm elections so far – but noted that “money doesn’t buy a race”.

“Trump put the tariffs on, cutting more jobs, hurting more people in our industry,” Howell added. “It’s billionaires versus the workers, and that’s the stance we’re making. They are getting rich and we’re paying for it. We’re paying for it out of our pockets.”

This article was amended on 23 September 2026 to clarify that more than $1.6bn has been poured into the 2026 midterm elections so far. An earlier version incorrectly stated it was $1.6tn.

Sports.title: Fury vs Joshua: Cardiff to host heavyweight fight on 11 December
Sports.text:
Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will contest their long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.

The bout, more than a decade in the making, will be broadcast globally on Netflix.

BBC Sport understands the main event could take place in the early hours of Saturday morning in the UK, with organisers considering a late start to cater for audiences in the United States.

Joshua and Fury will come face-to-face at a news conference in London on Wednesday, 30 September, as the build-up begins to one of the most anticipated fights in British boxing history.

"I am inspiring a generation," Joshua, 36, posted on Instagram. Fury, 38, is yet to comment on the announcement.

The event is being promoted as a collaboration between Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and UFC chief Dana White.

"Two of the best heavyweights of this generation, finally in the ring together," Alalshikh said.

"This will be one of the biggest fights in boxing history. I am very happy to make this fight happen for the fans."

The former two-time world champions had already signed contracts for the bout earlier this year, but the date and venue had yet to be confirmed.

London's Wembley Stadium and New York's Madison Square Garden were the frontrunners to stage the fight, but both presented issues before Cardiff recently emerged as an alternative.

The Principality Stadium has hosted late-night boxing before, including Joe Calzaghe's fight with Mikkel Kessler in November 2007, which began at 01:00 GMT.

Welsh Rugby Union and Cardiff Council officials welcomed the fight, saying it would reinforce the city's reputation for staging major events and could bring a significant economic boost, although some operational details still need to be finalised.

Joshua had been pushing for the fight to take place in the UK and has got his wish.

"Forever indebted to the UK public for their support of Anthony Joshua. We couldn't have got this over the line without you," his promoter Eddie Hearn said.

It is notable that White, who fronts Zuffa Boxing, is involved in the promotion.

"For more than a decade, boxing fans have been clamouring for the heavyweight showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. Together, they bring 66 wins, 52 knockouts and multiple heavyweight world titles into the ring," White said.

"On December 11, two of the biggest heavyweights of this generation finally collide - and the winner will take a significant place in heavyweight history."

There was no official statement from Hearn or Fury's promoter Frank Warren in the official news release sent by Netflix. Hearn had previously said he did not want White to be involved in promoting the fight.

A major fight in Cardiff taking place in the early hours might seem unusual, but there is precedent for UK events being scheduled around American television audiences.

Ricky Hatton's career-defining victory over Kostya Tszyu at Manchester's MEN Arena in June 2005 began at about 02:00 local time, allowing US broadcaster Showtime to show the fight on Saturday evening.

Less than a year later, Welshman Calzaghe's unification fight against Jeff Lacy at the same arena was staged at a similar hour. Calzaghe's 2007 victory over Kessler in Cardiff was also influenced by the US television schedule.

Mixed martial arts has gone even later. Michael Bisping's UFC title defence against Dan Henderson in Manchester in 2016 began deep into the night, with the fighters making their way to the octagon at about 04:45 local time.

When the UFC returned to Manchester in 2024, the UFC 304 main card began at 03:00 BST - corresponding with its traditional 22:00 start on the US east coast, with Briton Leon Edwards fighting Belal Muhammad in the main event just after 05:30.

The precise timing of Fury-Joshua has yet to be announced and promoter Eddie Hearn has played down suggestions it could begin as late as 03:00 GMT.

A ringwalk around 01:00 or 02:00 GMT would place the fight at 20:00 or 21:00 respectively on the US east coast.

For years, British boxing has debated who would win, watched negotiations collapse and wondered whether Fury and Joshua would ever actually share a ring.

Now, finally, there is a date and a venue. It's happening.

In many ways, the uncertainty of recent weeks was the Fury-Joshua story of the past decade in miniature.

In 2020, the two camps agreed the basis of a two-fight deal. In 2021, contracts were signed for an undisputed heavyweight contest, only for Deontay Wilder's successful arbitration case to force Fury into a third fight with the American. Then, in 2022, Joshua accepted a 60-40 split to challenge Fury, but that attempt also fell apart.

Joshua gets the British fight he wanted, organisers are given a stadium capable of staging a huge event in December and broadcasters can tailor it towards American audiences.

There is also an intriguing subplot in White's involvement. While it does not necessarily tell us who wielded the most influence behind the scenes, his involvement underlines just how many powerful figures were involved in finally putting this fight together.

What matters most for supporters is that Fury-Joshua will happen in Britain. There are some fights that are about more than purses, broadcast deals and site fees. This is one of them.

British fans have followed every twist: the world-title wins, the defeats, the comebacks, the rivalries and, above all, the failed attempts to make this contest.

Now they will have the chance to travel to Wales and say they were there. Tens of thousands will descend on the Principality Stadium for what will be one of the biggest nights British boxing has staged in years.

And somewhere among them may be a youngster attending their first fight, watching two of Britain's most recognisable sportsmen make their walks to the ring and deciding they want to lace up a pair of gloves themselves.

The fight may have arrived years later than many wanted but Fury-Joshua can still leave that kind of legacy.

Sports.title: Drinking at football matches - would fans welcome it?
Sports.text:
When UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham embarked on his trip to the United Nations in New York, he might not have been expecting a question about football fans drinking alcohol in grounds.

Burnham firmly believes the law that prevents supporters from having a beer at their seat during a match is outdated.

It's a position the Everton supporter has long held, and when asked was happy to reaffirm.

"I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination," said Burnham, who feels football fans are singled out compared to those of other sports and events.

There is no suggestion this is about to become official government policy, and last year MPs rejected a Conservative amendment to the Football Governance Bill that would have forced ministers to launch a formal consultation on scrapping the rule.

That was, of course, before Burnham returned to Downing Street.

It is a complicated and divisive issue, about not just safety. But is it something that match-going supporters actually want?

Drinking alcohol at football grounds in England and Wales has been strictly controlled since the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act was introduced in 1985.

It was brought in to counter escalating hooliganism through the 1970s and into the 1980s.

The ban impacts clubs in the Premier League down to the National League. While beer can be sold, it must be consumed in areas that do not have a view of the pitch.

Yet fans who support teams in the National League North and South and below can drink alcohol around the pitch.

The ban is more strict in Scotland, with a law in place since 1981 that alcohol is only available in hospitality areas and not for other fans.

It was initially imposed following a riot during the 1980 Scottish Cup final between Rangers and Celtic at Hampden.

However, attitudes have been changing in recent seasons.

It was lifted as part of a pilot scheme last year, with several Scottish clubs selling alcohol in clearly defined, monitored areas of the stadiums. It started with lower-level clubs, eventually being extended to the Premiership.

The Scotland national team joined the trial for the friendlies against Japan and Curacao earlier this year. It has been extended to games against Switzerland on 29 September and Slovenia next month.

The Women's Super League in England has just completed two seasons of successful trials and the rule preventing drinking in the stands has now been removed by the league's governing company, WSL Football.

The women's game is not governed by the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act, enabling the competition organiser to make the change.

Is there support for the move within English football's corridors of power?

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in August the competition had not "got a specific view" and "we'd need to give it some really careful thought".

The English Football League, however, issued a statement on Thursday that said it would be "receptive to discussions around reviewing the current legislation".

It added member clubs had already provided "a mandate to lobby for appropriate reform" which had "not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding".

The Football Supporters' Association has for some time backed changing the law.

Like the prime minister, it considers it to be unfair on football fans.

"I think it is outdated," FSA chairman Tom Greatrex told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme.

"If you go to watch football in Germany or in other places around the world, then it's perfectly acceptable.

"It is civilised and appropriate. There's no reason why that shouldn't be the case for football fans, as it is for fans of rugby league, watching Oasis, or anything else that happens often in the same stadiums in the same seats."

The FSA's position is that clubs should have the choice, in consultation with supporters, to sell alcohol.

Clubs might want to offer it in all stands, others in designated areas, while a few might choose not to do so at all.

Other sports offer designated alcohol-free sections, something that football clubs may wish to copy for some families and supporters who do not consume alcohol because of their religion.

The FSA acknowledges this, but believes having the option to make such decisions is important.

It believes relaxing the law would be more popular the further down the leagues you go, where alcohol sales could potentially provide a crucial additional income stream.

The UK Football Policing Unit rejected the suggestion, arguing alcohol plays "a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour" and that "other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour" that football does.

Yet for Greatrex, there is already proof police are not open to ideas through their previous opposition to safe standing.

Before it was introduced four years ago, Mark Roberts, who has been the national lead for football policing since 2014, told the BBC it would make it "easier to throw missiles, engage in hate chanting, racism, sneak alcohol in, take cocaine".

"[The police] were telling everybody that we couldn't have standing at football again, that it would jeopardise safety, " Greatrex said.

"Actually, what we saw then was a controlled, managed pilot projects to get that re-established.

"There hasn't been the level of disorder that some of the police sources were saying there would be. I think the police should have more of an open mind and engage in this in a sensible and mature way."

Football is in the only sport in the UK which faces restrictions on the consumption of alcohol.

Some of these sports have issues with alcohol-related and anti-social behaviour, but none have the same reputation as football.

The restrictions differ around Europe.

There is a strict ban in the top two divisions of Spanish football, where only alcohol-free beer can be sold outside of hospitality areas. It can, however, be taken to seats.

In the German Bundesliga, there is no ban on drinking at your seat. So relaxed is the approach to alcohol at games that you will even find people selling bottles of beer from shopping trolleys outside grounds.

In the Italian Serie A it is similarly as relaxed, though to a limit of 5% ABV. Some games which are designated "high risk" have sales suspended in and around the stadium.

In France, the Evin Law was introduced in 1991 which is pretty much in line with Scotland, as far as football is concerned. Alcohol cannot be sold at any sports event, other than in VIP areas.

Sports.title: Manchester City transfer news: Squad overhaul from a 650,000-strong database
Sports.text:
Inside the confines of Manchester City's sophisticated data operation is a fundamental phrase its experts work towards: "What does it take to win?"

In practice, the motto is broken down into three sections: identifying players, evaluating them and assessing how the club could improve them, all with a view to enhancing the statistical probability of City winning the Premier League.

Last season, the club's data department projected they would be there or thereabouts when it came to the title race, but their metrics indicated Arsenal were favourites to be champions. They were accurate.

This time around, City prefer to keep their projections under wraps - but five wins from five Premier League games have prompted predictions from supporters and pundits they will again be the Gunners' closest challengers.

City's devotion to data is at the heart of their efforts to close the gap on Arsenal and BBC Sport has been given unprecedent access to the inner workings of the club's metrics machine as we uncover some of the secrets guiding their work - particularly regarding player recruitment and sales.

Their work is a sign of the times in the Premier League, with clubs across the top flight and beyond increasingly using data for transfers and monitoring their teams' performance.

At City, one of the fundamental aims is to reduce risk of any market transaction, be it a purchase or a sale.

City grade players based on:

Overall characteristics;

The system they play in at their current club and how the manager is asking him and the team to play.

Once those four aspects are observed, City's aim is to understand not just how good the player is but how good he could become at the Etihad.

Since winning the Treble in 2023, City's squad has undergone a vast overhaul using this approach. Only four players from that historic campaign remain.

It is crucial to stress, however, that while data has made an indefinite impact on how City operate in the transfer market, the work of traditional scouts continues to be the primary gauge of whether they decide to move for a player.

"Data plays a role in our decision-making, but it is just one part of the overall picture," City sporting director Hugo Viana told BBC Sport.

"We know data cannot tell us everything about a player. It cannot fully show a person's character, mentality or behaviour.

"That is why we study data insights but focus on the expertise of our scouts and other specialists."

The prominence of data, however, has grown significantly behind the scenes at the Etihad.

Here BBC Sport can take you to the core of some of City's key transfer calls from their extensive three-year squad revamp - including the £116m signing of Elliot Anderson.

The starting point for any new signing is City's database of 650,000 footballers from around the world.

The next step is the brief: what sort of player is the club wanting to recruit.

This usually starts with a position, though that process isn't as simple as it sounds.

City, for example, categorise their full-backs into three types: those who are defensive, those who come inside, and those who play high and wide.

Once the club's data departments have the brief, filters that grade a player's overall ability are applied to whittle down the 650,000-man database to 20-50 names.

Juventus full-back Andrea Cambiaso is one player who has been on City's radar after the data highlighted him, particularly his ability to coming inside to build play in midfield.

That he is comfortable with both feet rated highly on the data, too.

In accordance with the data and the scouting reports it was decided the club would not proceed with their interest in Cambiaso in the previous window, but City's approach is likely to mean he will continue to be monitored.

The longlist of 20-50 names is cross-referenced with the scouting longlist. Generally there is a significant overlap between the players identified by data and the ones already on scouts' radar.

From there, further, more refined metrics are applied to rank and prioritise the longlist.

Scouts will then complete further diligence on the players to reduce the list to a maximum of about six players.

At this point, the club will complete deeper dives into the remaining players, including diligence on their injury record, athletic performance and behavioural habits.

The information is then collated into individual reports called acquisition packs which contain all the key metrics used to inform the decision on a player.

This includes a 'radar chart', which rates a range of specific on-field metrics.

For example, when Jeremy Doku was signed in 2023, then manager Pep Guardiola decided he wanted a winger who was direct, akin to Leroy Sane, because at the time they had Jack Grealish and Riyad Mahrez, who preferred to keep the ball and cut inside.

Among the criteria applied in City's brief were the following: making (running into) the box, pressure regains, take-on percentage and opposition-half pressure.

Doku's overall numbers ticked the boxes Guardiola was looking for, although the Belgian's 'making the box' score was among his lowest readings.

Since his arrival, Doku has improved this rating - an example City say shows how their data systems are helping to improve existing players.

There is also a 'utilisation chart' that records how often the player has been used over a three-year period, as well as a scouting grade that indicates how highly the traditional scouts rate the individual.

Each player is also awarded an overall "current impact score" - which predicts what impression he would be expected to make immediately on signing - and a "potential impact score" that projects the contribution the player could make in the future.

Perhaps the most intriguing reading on the acquisition packs is a player's "action value score". This positions them in a league table that includes City players and ones from rival clubs who play in a similar role.

Once the acquisition reports are evaluated, the list is further reduced to 2-3 players once City's valuation of the player has been factored in.

Data contributes heavily to the price range City believe a player falls in, and the valuation is never a single number.

A decision is then made on which player is the priority, though all players on the shortlist are worked on simultaneously in the event of changing circumstances, for example if a player becomes unavailable.

Indeed, being able to move according to the market is something the data team feel they have become adept at.

The sudden emergence of Yan Diomande last season led to City completing checks on him before he joined Real Madrid from RB Leipzig.

The club also paid close attention to Eduardo Camavinga's metrics in case Real decided to sell a midfielder.

Anderson was an obvious signing for a top Premier League club.

The 23-year-old had developed into a key player for Nottingham Forest. An added appeal was the fact he is English, and had cemented his position in the national team.

City fought off other top clubs, including Manchester United, to sign him.

It would seem, on the face of it, a straightforward decision.

But the way City analysed it underlines their incredibly forensic approach even when, outwardly, it might be considered they did not need to be so comprehensive given Anderson's obvious talents.

The fact they still used their algorithm and went through all their normal steps says a lot about elite football in the modern day - and also the limitations of data alone.

That is because - perhaps surprisingly - Anderson's metrics didn't necessarily catch the eye.

At the start of last season, despite emerging uncertainty over Guardiola's future, the club knew they would be in the market for at least one central midfielder come the summer.

They knew Bernardo Silva was leaving while there were doubts over the futures of Rodri and Nico Gonzalez.

There was an acknowledgement that replacing Silva and Rodri like-for-like would be virtually impossible, so they looked for a player who was equally adept at building play from either deep or high central midfield.

As last season developed, doubt also emerged over the future of Tijjani Reijnders - but Enzo Fernandez was viewed as the favoured replacement for the Dutchman.

Anderson made the initial cut from the 650,000-man database to the longlist - but was not high in that group. However, his metric readings didn't immediately scream out the "no-brainer" he ultimately became.

As City took a closer look, there was an acknowledgement Anderson's case does highlight some of the limitations of data.

Anderson did not score lots of goals for Forest, or consistently provide assists. Because, generally speaking, Forest aren't a possession team like City, his general metrics in their algorithm did not grab the attention.

With that in mind, City's data analysts had to consider that, because Anderson was generally playing closer to his own goal than he would at City, he wasn't getting the opportunities to impress in the final third of the pitch.

So they paid close attention to what he was doing at Forest and modelled his potential role in a City team that generally plays closer to the opposition's goal, dominates possession and has more elite players.

Among the criteria graded on Anderson's 'radar chart' were defensive regains, duel success, line-breaking passes, aerial-duel success and defensive errors.

With his reading for defensive errors, it was acknowledged that, because Forest were a transitional side, some were a result of the area of the pitch in which he was asked to operate.

He may, for example, have regained possession deep inside his own half but lost the ball because he had to play a longer and a riskier pass after being asked to play forward quickly.

In the same scenario at City, it is anticipated Anderson would have options to play a shorter pass with a greater success rate.

"Just because a player doesn't have the opportunity to perform a particular action on a regular basis because of the team he is playing doesn't mean he can't do it," said a source.

Anderson's data readings improved significantly as the season developed, which compelled the club's scouts to watch him on a regular basis.

He stood up very favourably against City's existing midfielders - and a list of rival players the club had identified as possible signings in that area.

The results of the diligence completed by City's data team, scouts and other experts meant that even though Anderson's price increased beyond what City believed was his true valuation, they felt the risk was low.

"Elliot Anderson is a great example of how the process works," Viana said.

"The data was positive for Elliot and gave us real confidence in his profile, but it was the insight from our scouts and wider performance team that helped us understand the player and his attributes and this proved our belief that he was the right fit for the club."

BBC Sport was also provided with fascinating insight into how data was used to sign Julian Alvarez from River Plate for £14m in 2022.

The initial recommendation came from scouts, and given Alvarez was not a player originally identified by his metrics, the data team had to take a closer look.

Because the Argentine league isn't recognised as one of the strongest globally, City's general data settings mean players will reach a natural ceiling with their readings in comparison to those playing in one of Europe's top five divisions.

So, City dug deeper into Alvarez's stats, and his impact on both the ball and River's scorelines.

The stats showed he was by far the best player in the Argentine top flight, and City believed they had enough evidence to say he would develop into a starter for a top-half club in one of Europe's top five leagues within two-and-half years.

The data model valued Alvarez between £26m and £40m. City signed him for £14m so believed they were signing an undervalued player.

Alvarez's projected value was £70m after three years. They eventually sold him to Atletico Madrid in 2024 for £81m.

The signing of Abdukodir Khusanov from Lens also provides intriguing insight into City's reliance on data.

The 22-year-old didn't initially make City's 50-man longlist, but on closer inspection they found while his output on the ball needed to improve, his physical data - for example his covering runs behind - was through the roof.

Khusanov's on-the-ball metrics, City say, have improved significantly since he signed in January 2025.

The departure of Guardiola and the arrival of Enzo Maresca is not expected to alter the club's approach significantly.

The key metrics Maresca looks for in a player are understood to be very similar to Guardiola's, with the notable difference that the Italian prefers his full-backs to be more direct.

Rooted in City's coach recruitment process is a certain team philosophy and way of playing, with any new manager expected to produce a side that is possession dominant, can press high, regain possession high up the pitch, produce quality chances and entertain.

That philosophy was designed before Guardiola's appointment, and the Spaniard produced the purest form of City's footballing ideology.

With that in mind, the change in manager has not drastically altered the way City's data department approach their work.

Maresca will continue to work closely with them as he looks to build his own dynasty - but much of the hard work in building a squad to last is complete.

Before City's Treble-winning season, the internal data indicators were such that the club knew they would soon need to overhaul a squad that had reached its peak.

Selling players such as Kevin de Bruyne, Kyle Walker, Riyad Mahrez and Ilkay Gundogan wasn't easy given their illustrious service and the fact they were still performing at a very high level.

Data, though, allows the club to spot declining trends well in advance - often two or three years - before a player is offloaded.

Those particular metrics help City identify when the right time is to sell a player is - perhaps even before the buying club have spotted a drop in performance.

And when those trends are identified, the club can plan well in advance.

From there the club decide whether to start embedding a player from the academy or enter the market to replace.

Ayyoub Bouaddi's arrival from Lille this summer is a prime example. At 18, City realise he isn't necessarily going to have a profound impact this season - but the club believe the Moroccan will be able to make a bigger contribution within two years.

After the Treble season, the recruitment remit at City was to lower the average age of the squad and build a set of players that could deliver sustained success.

But doing that at City comes with a catch. Because at City, the team are always expected to compete for trophies.

Lowering the age of a squad is one thing; doing so while continuing to win is far more complicated.

In previous years, for example, City's data systems identified former Brighton trio Moises Caicedo, Marc Cucurella and Carlos Baleba, who have been lauded as data successes.

But there was a sense at City that the development of such signings would take too long for them to make an impact on a team that has the remit of winning titles or assets that could be developed and sold for a profit.

City have successfully lowered the average age of the squad to the extent they now have the third youngest set of players in the Premier League behind Newcastle and Chelsea.

But with the signings of goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, defender Marc Guehi, and Fernandez and Anderson they have added players who can not only grow with that new generation but also already have vast experience of top-level football.

City's data indicates their current squad will not peak for another two to three years - but also projects they are likely be among the title challengers this season.

Time will tell if they are right.

Sports.title: Premier League Bermuda Triangle: Do stats back Brighton, Bournemouth, Brentford social media theory?
Sports.text:
It's the place where points are lost and never to be seen again, according to a popular social media meme.

Draw a line from Brighton to Bournemouth to Brentford and back down to Brighton again and you will have formed the Premier League's very own "Bermuda Triangle".

Those three clubs have developed a reputation for taking points off the traditional Big Six - Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham.

Recent results have only fuelled the narrative and helped to push the tongue-in-cheek theory.

On Friday night, Brentford beat Chelsea 3-0. Less than 24 hours later, Brighton outclassed champions Arsenal, albeit by the same scoreline - though it was a victory that could arguably have been even more emphatic had David Raya not produced a couple of smart saves.

Bournemouth, meanwhile, pushed Liverpool all the way before falling to a gritty 1-0 defeat, with Alisson forced into a brilliant recovery stop to deny the Cherries an early opener.

Those are the sort of performances that stick in supporters' minds and help explain why the theory has taken hold.

To a point.

Since the start of the 2024-25 season, Brighton have been the best-performing non-traditional Big Six side against Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Man City, Manchester United and Spurs, taking 42 points from 26 games - an average of 1.62 points per match.

The Cherries are not far behind, collecting 35 points from 26 matches, or 1.35 points per game.

Brentford, however, have taken 22 points from 26 matches, averaging 0.85 points per game. Newcastle (1.46), Nottingham Forest (1.46) and Aston Villa (1.38) have all matched or outperformed the Bees against the traditional Big Six over the same period.

In other words, the clubs most commonly grouped together by the meme have produced very different levels of success against elite opposition.

Brighton and Bournemouth have consistently taken points off the Premier League's heavyweights. Brentford's record is less convincing.

In fact, the Opta data suggests Brighton are the main reason the theory has gained such traction.

Since Fabian Hurzeler took charge, only Kenny Dalglish's Blackburn have recorded a better points-per-game return against the traditional Big Six among managers of non-Big-Six clubs with at least 10 matches.

The popularity of the Bermuda Triangle idea may say as much about perception as results.

When it comes to recruitment and spending, Bournemouth, Brighton and Brentford operate in a different world to the Premier League's biggest clubs. They cannot simply outspend Arsenal, Liverpool or Manchester City.

That makes their victories more memorable. Upsets also tend to linger longer in the memory because they fit a familiar story: well-run clubs outperforming opponents with significantly greater resources.

The meme is not entirely without foundation, although the evidence is considerably stronger for Brighton and Bournemouth than it is for Brentford.

Brentford's overall record is weaker, although a series of eye-catching victories under Thomas Frank and now Keith Andrews have helped cement their reputation as a difficult opponent for elite clubs. And the start to this season has helped: their Chelsea success added to by an opening day 3-0 rout of Spurs.

Sports.title: Asian Games: eSports star Yuki Kurihara, 11, aims to become youngest medallist
Sports.text:
Primary school student Yuki Kurihara made a flying start as he became the youngest athlete at this year's Asian Games.

The 11-year-old eSports star beat opponents almost three times his age in his native Japan on Thursday.

The youngster competes in Puyo Puyo Champions, a puzzle game similar to Tetris which was developed in Japan.

Players try to clear their screen of coloured blobs by lining them up and popping them, creating chain reactions called 'dairensa'.

Kurihara beat all four opponents to top Group A and he will attempt to win gold on Saturday.

"The best feeling in the world is winning," Kurihara told the Japan Times., external "When I lose, I cry and try not to think about it too much. When the play doesn't go well it's not fun, so I want to quit. But I always come back.

"I hope to win a gold medal for Japan."

Japan's youngest athlete in Asian Games history could also become the competition's youngest ever medallist.

Indonesia's Bunga Nyimas holds the record, having won bronze in women's skateboarding aged 12 in 2018.

eSports has appeared in the previous two editions of the Asian Games, with Puyo Puyo being one of 11 medal events this year.

Kurihara says he eats eel to prepare for contests and secured his place on the Japan team at just 10 years old.

In February he beat an adult professional to win Sega's Puyo Puyo Grand Prix Final and he turned pro himself in April - two months before his 11th birthday.

The Asian Games are being held in Nagoya and the wider Aichi area from 19 September to 4 October.

Sports.title: Laver Cup 2026: Carlos Alcaraz on US Open run, injury and Jannik Sinner rivalry
Sports.text:
Most players, after seeing their US Open title defence end at 3:34am after five intense sets, would not walk away smiling.

Carlos Alcaraz is not most players.

After his loss to Ben Shelton - a match that played out over a gruelling four hours and 28 minutes - the Spaniard was filmed walking down the Arthur Ashe tunnel with a huge grin on his face.

Alcaraz had been competing in his first tournament for over five months after suffering a wrist injury that left him in pain every day.

He did not defend his French Open title or compete at Wimbledon, and did not know if he would play in New York until a week before.

"The quarter-final was great - it was a gift for me," Alcaraz told BBC Sport before this week's Laver Cup in London.

"I suffered, but I enjoyed and that's why I smiled when I walked out of the court because I missed that feeling."

The match against Shelton was the latest finish in the tournament's history, and was one of several matches at Flushing Meadows to finish in the early hours.

Eventual champion Alexander Zverev finished past 1am in three of his first five matches, while Venus Williams finished her first-round match at 2am.

"I think it's too much," Alcaraz said of playing so late.

"The last match people stayed but if that match was played earlier, the court could have been packed.

"I would like to change the schedule a little with a maximum finish at 11pm or whatever would be better."

Alcaraz, 23, is one of a number of players to have missed large chunks of the season with injury.

Britain's Jack Draper has had a lengthy struggle with an arm injury, ultimately ending his season early to recover, while Alcaraz's rival Jannik Sinner missed the US Open with a knee injury.

The Spaniard said at the US Open that he will miss some tournaments in the future to allow himself to be "mentally and physically healthy".

He will compete for Team Europe in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London this week, between 25-27 September.

The team tournament pits Europe - captained by Yannick Noah - against a World team overseen by Andre Agassi.

"When you have your team-mates, the best in the world, by your side, it's a weird feeling but it's beautiful," Alcaraz said.

"We played like our lives depend on it. That's why the Laver Cup is so good to watch as well."

Alcaraz and Italy's Sinner split eight Grand Slam titles between them from 2024 and 2025, establishing a generational rivalry in the process.

They have only met once this year because of injuries, with Sinner winning their sole meeting in the Monte Carlo Masters final to become world number one.

"I have text him not too much, but a few times when he has been winning everything, mostly at the beginning of the year," Alcaraz added.

"I miss him, I miss seeing him around, playing against him. He pushes me to be a better player.

"People will be waiting for those matches, so I think it's going to be better."

Sports.title: England v New Zealand: Maddie Feaunati returns to back row for hosts
Sports.text:
Maddie Feaunati returns to bring big-game experience and dynamism to the back row as England take on a resurgent New Zealand, their closest challengers at the top of the world rankings, in front of more than 50,000 fans at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.

Feaunati comes in at number eight, with Alex Matthews shifting to blind-side flanker and Abi Burton to the bench.

The three starters all featured in England's Women's Rugby World Cup final win against Canada, one year ago on Sunday.

England, whose 39-match winning streak was halted by a 26-26 draw against Canada last weekend, make their other changes in the front row.

Props Mackenzie Carson and Sarah Bern come in to start with Hannah Botterman and Maud Muir poised to add power off the bench.

Bryony Field, whose involvement in the international set-up before this autumn was limited to age-grade appearances half a decade ago, retains her place at starting hooker ahead of May Campbell.

Amy Cokayne and Connie Powell are both missing through injury, while Lark Atkin Davies has only recently given birth.

England's backline remains unchanged with Helena Rowland at inside centre and Jess Breach, Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and Ellie Kildunne making up the back three.

Natasha Hunt, Tatyana Heard and Emma Sing are the specialist backs on the bench.

Sports.title: Asian Games: Shin Ohashi, 17, breaks 200m breaststroke world record
Sports.text:
Japanese teenager Shin Ohashi broke the 200m breaststroke world record at the Asian Games, despite contracting Covid-19 in the build-up.

Ohashi, 17, won in two minutes 4.83 seconds to comfortably break the previous record of 2:05.48, which was set by China's Qin Haiyang at the 2023 World Championships.

Ohashi is the second teenage prodigy to make headlines during these Games after China's Yu Zidi, 13, won her third gold on Wednesday.

It is his second gold of the Games after he shared the 100m breaststroke title with China's Dong Zhihao earlier this week.

"Regarding Covid, after all, there was a part where it created a little anxiety for me mentally," Ohashi said after his victory.

"But, conversely, physically I think it was good that I was able to properly rest my body as a period ​of recovery."

Ohashi won five golds at the World Junior Championships last year, with France's Leon Marchand, the sensation in the pool at the 2024 Paris Olympics, describing the youngster as a "scary" prospect.

Meanwhile, Zhang Zhanshuo, 19, won his sixth gold of the Games as China won the 4x100m freestyle relay.

Sports.title: Women's Champions League: What we learned from return of Europe's top tier competition
Sports.text:
The Women's Champions League returned this week and with it came a host of unanswered questions for the ambitious English trio involved.

Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City all have designs on winning the competition and, on the face of it, got their campaigns off to solid starts.

Arsenal and Chelsea both have three points after narrow home wins while City recovered from 2-0 down for a creditable draw at heavyweights Bayern Munich.

But scratch deeper, and this was an unconvincing week, particularly given last season's finalists Barcelona and Lyon both opened with commanding victories.

Are the Women's Super League clubs equipped to challenge this season? What still needs addressing? And who has the best chance of lifting the trophy in Warsaw next May?

Last season, Manchester City exploited their absence from European competition to romp to the Women's Super League title.

In returning to the elite tier this season, their squad will face greater tests, and that was immediately true when 2025-26 semi-finalists Bayern Munich raced into a two-goal lead.

But Andree Jeglertz's team gave an immediate indication they belong at this level by recovering to draw 2-2, with summer signings Beth Mead and Carlotta Wamser justifying their arrival at the champions with their first goals for the club.

That was crucial given usual goalscorer Khadija Shaw surprisingly proved fallible in missing a penalty.

When she inevitably finds her shooting boots, City should be just fine in this competition.

With only two goals and five points from three matches, it has been an inauspicious start to the season for Arsenal, who have been bullish in targeting trophies.

Up against Danish minnows HB Koge, it was not just the Disney+ TV coverage of the game that was marred by glitches.

Arsenal's expected goals tally of 1.93 does not tell the story of a performance that was dominant with the ball, but they only fashioned two shots on target against a side they were expected to beat comfortably.

Boss Renee Slegers made a raft of changes, including resting Alessia Russo, but the eight forwards she ultimately featured struggled to breach the resolute visitors' backline, with the Gunners requiring a 95th-minute penalty to steal the points.

Dismissing lower-ranked teams at the start of competition has been an Achilles' heel for Arsenal and, while they did win, tougher tests await and Slegers needs to find a solution.

Sports.title: Debbie Beard and Amanda Thorpe lost their husbands - this is their story
Sports.text:
Warning: This story contains discussion of suicide and information some readers may find distressing

Where do they even begin?

Two women, united in grief, are meeting for the first time.

Debbie Beard lost her husband just over a year ago. Matt Beard, the former Liverpool Women manager, died in hospital on 20 September 2025. He is believed to have taken his own life, though an inquest is yet to conclude.

Amanda Thorpe's husband Graham, the former England and Surrey cricketer, took his own life in 2024. He had "spiralled into depression" after losing his job as a batting coach in 2022.

The two women, who had never met before, came together at an event launched by the Prince of Wales and the Royal Foundation to urge sport at every level to make suicide prevention part of its culture through a new nationwide toolkit.

There they spoke to the BBC's business editor Simon Jack, who was 17 when his father took his own life.

On Your Side, external is a set of resources available online that aims "to make suicide prevention as much a part of sport as warm-up, training and performance".

Amanda Thorpe has said previously she believes her husband would still be alive had he received more support from the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) after leaving his coaching role. Following the inquest into his death, the ECB said it was "a profound tragedy" and added Thorpe's passing was a "stark reminder" of the challenges many face with mental health.

Matt Beard died a month after leaving his role as manager of Burnley Women. He had been in the post for only two months. When the inquest into his death was postponed indefinitely, Burnley said they were "aware of an ongoing legal process" and would "not be making any comment at this time".

Amanda: "Graham had been struggling for the previous year to 18 months during Covid. Graham didn't really like following rules and there were quite a few in Covid - like playing under bubble conditions. So he had been having some medication and therapy in his job. But then Graham lost his job and he didn't see it coming.

"He did pride himself with having been in the game his whole life. He just couldn't believe that he was blindsided by it.

"I think at least two other people were sacked at the same time, which does happen at the end of disastrous Ashes series.

"Also he was probably drinking too much and found the whole of the last trip in Covid very stressful. He then took a playful video at the end of the tour, when they had a few drinks with the opposition. One of the players sent it to two friends and someone unfortunately leaked it, so it was in the Sydney Morning Herald."

Simon: "Going for a few drinks with the opposition - you would think that that happens in sport all the time, but they lost?"

Amanda: "Yes. It's OK if you win but you're not allowed to have a drink if you lose. He was probably in shock. He couldn't believe it. And he was embarrassed and ashamed about this stupid video, which to me he blew way out of proportion. But he was in this tunnel where he thought he'd messed it all up. So he went into a quick and steep decline."

Simon: "During that period, what could have been done? You said that he was seeking some help. What might have made a difference, do you think?"

Amanda: "He was having therapy sessions. He had 10 sessions. There's obviously the confidentiality but I found out after he made a very serious attempt on his life, when he really hurt himself very badly, that he'd mentioned suicide. I didn't know about that at the time. Of course, I feel that if I'd known, things could have been different. And I did feel that he wasn't really getting better. It was difficult. I felt like maybe he did need more help - maybe residential but we didn't really know where to find that."

Simon: "Debbie, Matt also lost his job..."

Simon: "Were there any signs that he was struggling with mental health, and then was there a steep decline afterwards?"

Debbie: "I think there were changes in behaviour, looking back. Performance-wise the team weren't doing well so there was a lot of abuse on social media. He could never really speak his truth during media interviews of what was going on behind the scenes and he used to sound off to me at home.

"I've found out since that he had spoken to his brother quite a lot about his mental health. But whenever I would say to Matt 'how are things?', he'd be, 'I'm all right, I'm all right', because he always wanted the best for other people.

"He didn't want to concern me and the family that he was having these thoughts and that he was going through these different struggles.

"The sacking came out of the blue and there was a lot of speculation around that. He was starting to drink more than he would have done normally. In terms of his behaviour, I would say he was taking a lot of risks as well. So maybe that was the start of this with him."

Amanda: "Graham was known as a tough competitor. He was a very happy person and loved life, but it can happen to anyone. He wasn't thinking straight really because everything kind of became a vortex. And he just sort of lost the ability to be able to be grounded and think straight. Also you think you're thinking straight when you're not."

Simon: "One of the things about sport that's been discussed is that its reach is enormous. Coaches have a very intimate and closely proximate relationship with people. They can see what's going on with them - even at grassroots level. What would you encourage people to do if they see other people struggling, either in their family or in their community?"

Debbie: "It's a very difficult conversation. It's very hard. But if you're with these people day in, day out, you notice the changes in them. Matt was very intuitive with his players - he could sense things if they weren't playing right. He might have had a conversation with them just one-to-one, away from everyone else, and then make suggestions. There's an awful lot of emphasis on the physical side of someone's wellbeing, but not the mental side. That needs to be explored with people."

Simon: "It's a tough conversation to have, isn't it? Even with your nearest and dearest, let alone with someone on the team. I wonder whether Matt found it difficult when he had to sack players or drop them from the team.

Debbie: "He did. He used to come home and say: 'I've had a hard conversation today with such and such, I've had to let them go and there were tears.' And he'd say: 'I feel guilty.' He was the one who had to deliver the news. He felt tremendous guilt about letting people go."

Simon: "What did Graham's friends in the game come and say to you afterwards? You must have known them - you would have been part of that community."

Amanda: "They were really sad and really gutted. When he was really ill he was ashamed and he shut a lot of people out. So it was hard to get through to him. He would say: 'I've lost all my friends.' And I'm like: 'You haven't.' You know that's his brain. 'You haven't lost your friends at all,' I'd say. But that's how he felt. He felt very isolated."

Simon: "Did Graham have high highs and low lows? I mean, when he scored 100 against Australia or whatever? I just wonder whether he was a person of heightened emotions?"

Amanda: "He always used to say: 'Don't get too down about it... it might not be your day.' And I think if you're going to be like that, then when there are the highs you don't go overboard. He'd say it's his job but it is difficult with people scrutinising what you're doing and everything."

Simon: "What is it that you hope comes out of talking to us and what the Royal Foundation is doing?"

Debbie: "I think with the Royal Foundation, it is exposing the issue and people are going to be talking about it. But there needs to be the right support for when people need it - when they ask for that help.

"It's just making sure that toolkit is followed through and there are people that you can connect with and talk to.

"A connection with a therapist is a difficult one because it's someone you're going to be opening a box to. You want to let everything out but you need to trust that therapist. So it's making sure that there's a good connection there as well - that you feel comfortable talking about your innermost feelings."

Simon: "This is pretty raw for you. Why do you think it's important to talk to the world about this?"

Debbie: "For me and my children, we don't want another family to go through this. It is pretty raw and it's not just the grief, it's the practical side. You've lost a second income. I've still got to pay the same amount of rent, bills, etc. It is the practicality of it and you're juggling all the time - making sure the children are OK... still doing the school runs."

Simon: "You're obviously sad. Are you're angry? Determined?"

Amanda: "I'm angry at myself as well - the guilt you have. 'Why didn't I say that?' And you've got all these 'what ifs'. So all of that nonsense. And, yes - angry as well. 'Couldn't we just have done something?' But, you know, we fall. You know I'm his wife and I still didn't expect that to happen and I ask why he had to go through such a horrible thing. You wouldn't wish it on your worst enemy - and then there's the family as well - my daughters.

"My youngest went off to uni and then Emma went too. So it was just me and the geriatric dog. So it was quite hard."

Debbie: "It's going to be a long road."

Simon: "But it's a road you're both on and I think it's a road you've helped a lot of people with by talking to us."

Debbie: "We've got each other. We've met today and we are going to meet again."

Amanda: "Yes, be a force to be reckoned with! Isn't that what they say?"

Debbie: "Yeah, so I'll come down to you, you come up to me. We're part of this club that we never wanted to be in but we are going to make people listen to what we've got to say. We just want to make a change and help people and just highlight it - we never want anyone else to be in this position. We're going to go great guns aren't we?"

If you are suffering distress or despair, details of help and support are available at BBC Action Line.

Sports.title: Have Arsenal been figured out? Three big questions after Brighton’s upset
Sports.text:
Before this past weekend, Arsenal had not lost in the Premier League since April. Nine straight league wins had been enough to crown the Gunners as champions at the end of last season and firmly establish them as the team to beat early this season.

Against Brighton on Saturday, though, the team to beat were beaten. Thoroughly.

Arsenal weren’t just pecked by the Seagulls. They were pressed to death by them. Usually so resilient, even in the face of such opposition exuberance, the Premier League champions fell apart on the south coast, losing a match by three goals for the first time in over three years. It was jarring to see Arsenal so out of sorts.

Was this simply a Control-Alt-Delete game for Arsenal, or has the manner of the Seagulls’ performance provided a template for others to use? Was Saturday merely a blip that the Gunners will quickly recover from or the first crack in their previously impenetrable armour? Let’s tackle those and some other questions from the Premier League’s big upset before the international break.

How did Brighton do it?

The most effective element of Brighton’s performance was their relentless pressing of Arsenal in periods of settled possession. While the Seagulls still had pressing triggers which prompted them to push high up the pitch at certain moments, Fabian Hürzeler also recognised the need to prevent the champions from getting to the edge of the box. They were in Arsenal’s faces for most of the match.

Brighton defensive midfielder Chema Andrés pushed up on to Martin Ødegaard whenever he could, moving Brighton into a man-to-man shape against the ball and limiting the Norwegian whenever he dropped deep. Faced with a four-on-four situation in build-out, Arsenal simply weren’t sharp enough on the ball to get around the press, forcing David Raya to go long more times than he would have liked. From there, Brighton could turn the ball over and attack at speed in the other direction.

This made the match a transition-heavy affair which suited Brighton’s attacking players. Focal point Charalampos Kostoulas was an all-round threat while Pascal Gross, Maxim De Cuyper and Diego Gómez were impactful in open space. Hürzeler’s approach never allowed the game state to shift in Arsenal’s favour. He covered all bases.

Is Brighton’s formula replicable?

Maybe, but it will be tough. Hürzeler’s team are a physical force of nature. Of the four players that covered the most distance on Saturday, three were Brighton players and it’s these legs and lungs that allows them to press so hard for so long. No Premier League team is averaging more high turnovers per 90 minutes this season. Not every team can do what Brighton do.

For all that Brighton’s approach as a team, and a club, epitomises the modern game, there was an old school quality to the way they disrupted Arsenal. “We wanted to win the small battles first,” explained Hürzeler on talkSport, revealing the instructions he gave his players. “Win the first header, win the first tackle, win the first throw-in, win the first corner.”

Should Arsenal fans be worried?

Probably not, since there were some mitigating factors that explain Arsenal’s underperformance. The trip to Brighton was their fourth away game in just 10 days, and their general lethargy reflected this. Furthermore, many of Arsenal’s best players, including Martin Ødegaard, Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka, were denied a pre-season due to their extended involvement at the World Cup.

Two of Brighton’s three goals came from low-xG shots from outside the box. Arsenal were guilty of not closing the space for the shooter quickly enough, but on another day Gross and Kostoulas would have shot over the bar rather than into the top corner. Indeed, Brighton’s three goals came from a total xG of just 1.31, less than Arsenal’s xG of 1.63.

Arsenal are also still without the injured William Saliba whose presence next to Gabriel Magalhaes surely would have steadied their defensive line. Without Ben White in the lineup, the Gunners additionally lacked the chemistry down the right wing that has been such a feature of their early-season success. Saka was a non-factor in the game.

Many predicted Arsenal would stroll this season’s title race. They still might. While Manchester City are now top of the table, Arsenal are two points better off now than they were at the same stage of last season when they went on to win the title for the first time since the Arsène Wenger era. Until Saturday, they had won seven out of seven in all competitions this season. Mikel Arteta need not panic.

You can bet, however, that the tactical analysts and data crunchers employed by Arsenal’s rivals will have closely watched Brighton’s 3-0 win more than a few times by the time club soccer resumes next month.

Sports.title: Japan teenager Shin Ohashi overcomes Covid and fever to smash breaststroke world record
Sports.text:
The Japanese teenager Shin Ohashi said a bout of Covid helped him smash the men’s 200m breaststroke world record in a time of 2min 4.83sec at the Asian Games on Thursday.

The 17-year-old won his second gold of the Games in Tokyo despite running a temperature of about 39C just days before the competition began.

The win continued his stunning rise in the sport and marked him out as the man to beat at the Los Angeles Olympics in two years’ time.

Ohashi said his illness had been a blessing in disguise after cutting more than half a second off the previous world record, held by China’s Qin Haiyang, which had stood since July 2023. “With the Covid, it made me feel uneasy mentally,” he said. “But on the other hand it meant I was forced to rest my body properly for a while. I think that was a good thing.”

Ohashi had already won the 100m breaststroke gold this week in Tokyo after a dead heat with China’s Dong Zhihao. He will try to make it a hat-trick when he swims in Friday’s 50m breaststroke.

Ohashi took control from the off in the 200m final and from then it was a race against the clock. He finished 3.84sec faster than the silver medallist Denis Petrashov of Kyrgyzstan.

“My next goal is to win gold at next year’s world championships and then go on to win gold at the Olympics,” said Ohashi. “I don’t want to be satisfied and I want to feel these emotions again.”

Ohashi’s success has seen him tipped to follow in the footsteps of the Japanese breaststroke great Kosuke Kitajima. The “Frog King” won the 100m-200m double at the 2004 Athens Olympics and repeated the feat four years later in Beijing.

Ohashi said he was “watching all the other swimmers and trying to learn from them”. He continued: “I don’t really have any heroes, I think all swimmers are fantastic. But in terms of achievements, Kitajima is the one I would like to emulate most.”

Gaming_Tech.title: Why did an OpenAI system hack Australia's health system - and can it be stopped in the future?
Gaming_Tech.text:
The hack was carried out by an AI agent - an autonomous computer program that uses AI to complete a task with minimal human oversight.

On 18 June one of OpenAI's agents went rogue during a test exercise - the company has said it was supposed to "look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation".

In the process it "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said.

OpenAI said it only realised the breach had happened at all in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity", and the company sent an email to a generic Australian government inbox some weeks later.

That email seems to have gone unnoticed for five days before it was escalated to Australia's cyber-security experts on 10 September.

The prime minister described the breach as "obviously unacceptable" and said OpenAI took "way too long" to inform Australian officials.

Analysts have also raised concerns over OpenAI's almost three-month delay in noticing and reporting the breach via email.

"The way the notice arrived bothers me as much as the delay," chief data and AI officer Simon Liu from cyber-security firm TrustDecision told the BBC.

Australia has said this incident is the first of its kind, and experts agree it might be.

As far as we know, hacks carried out by AI agents are still quite rare occurrences - but then again, it is largely up to companies themselves to disclose them.

Hacks like this have happened before. In July, OpenAI agents went rogue during a test and infiltrated tech start-up Hugging Face's internal systems.

The AI agents decided that ignoring the limits on what should be done to achieve their goal was the best course of action.

This is what the industry calls "misalignment" - broadly defined as when AI machines do not act in humanity's best interests, such as by bending the rules.

It is a problem that is fundamental to making AI safe, and it is proving challenging.

To put it simply, the type of AI models at play here - known as large language models - are designed to predict the likeliest output to a given input, rather than consider the consequences of that output as a human would.

Companies attempt to prevent negative consequences by placing "guardrails" on the AI but, as the Australian government found out, that is not always enough.

Dr Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at the University of New South Wales Institute for Cyber Security, told the BBC this sort of hack would likely "grow in severity and in frequency", adding: "I do hope that this incident does start ringing alarm bells in governments around the world."

Niusha Shafiabady, professor of computational intelligence at the Australian Catholic University, said this incident had shown the need to "judge autonomous AI by its behaviour under pressure, not by the promises in a product launch".

"The deeper technical risk is that autonomous AI does not always know when it is wrong, and humans may not be able to see why it made a decision," she said.

"Without strong verification and hard boundaries, probabilistic errors can quietly become operational failures."

As warnings mount about the potentially devastating impact of AI, many in the industry and in governments around the world are openly wondering about what national and international regulations might be needed to keep it in check.

Meanwhile some scientists, experts and workers have dismissed the bleak projections as vague, hypothetical, or an effort by large AI developers to ensure their dominance.

As it stands, AI companies largely regulate themselves - but this week, 20 nations, including Australia and Canada, signed a joint statement calling for better safeguards, globally consistent standards, and an international regulator off the back of these concerns.

However, the US and China, two nations at the forefront of AI development, have so far resisted calls for greater regulation, raising questions over whether this hack will be the first of many, or the wake up call many experts want it to be.

"The immediate harm here appears limited, but the governance lesson is not," says Dr Raffaele Fabio Ciriello, senior lecturer in business information systems at the University of Sydney.

"As AI agents become more capable and autonomous, those capabilities need to be matched by proportionate containment, real-time monitoring, clear accountability, independent oversight, and much faster incident reporting."

Additional reporting by Tom Gerken and Joe Tidy

Gaming_Tech.title: They were labelled 'pervert glasses'. Will Meta's camera-free version change their image?
Gaming_Tech.text:
When Meta first launched its AI-powered smart glasses in 2023, in collaboration with the sunglasses brand Ray-Ban, it unleashed a storm of controversy.

There have been multiple reports of the devices being used to harass women and girls in particular, filming them without their consent, then sharing the footage.

The image problem doesn't seem to have been cured by Meta's enlistment this summer of Kylie Jenner, Kim Kardashian's sister, as their prime model. The devices have been dubbed "pervert" or "creepy" glasses. In the UK, JD Wetherspoon pubs, a handful of major theatres, Comic-Con, some schools, and Faslane, home of the UK's nuclear submarines, have all chosen to ban them.

On Thursday, Meta is unveiling a new version which does not contain a camera at all, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio. They will have the audio functions of the original glasses - including the ability to make phone calls or play music, with the sound funnelled directly into your ear - but with fewer implications for privacy.

To some in the industry, it looks like an interesting pivot - a response, perhaps, to the backlash over privacy.

The tech giant denies that the new glasses have been rushed out in response to public anger. They say the product has been in development for two years. The audio-only version is cheaper than its camera-enabled cousins, and Meta says it has a lighter frame and better battery life.

When I put it to Meta Glasses' head of product Ankit Brahmbhatt that I thought they might overtake the original camera-enabled glasses in sales, there was a pregnant pause.

"We have, I think, something for everyone," he said, choosing his words very carefully.

Does the release of a camera-free option represent a shift in how tech companies see the future of smart glasses? And is Meta's original vision getting further away?

Or should we see camera-free glasses as a niche side-product that serves a small market - a bit like how some mobile manufacturers are now releasing internet-disabled "brick" phones for people who are tired of social media?

There's no doubt that smart glasses have become controversial.

I was lent a pair of Meta Ray-Bans – with cameras - to try out. I was initially nervous about wearing them in public, in case someone got physical: I have heard of people knocking them off wearers' heads and smashing them in the street.

The reality was that I wore them on public transport and on foot in several cities including London, Glasgow and Portsmouth, and nobody batted an eyelid. It made me wonder whether awareness of them is really as high as both Meta and anti-glasses campaigners believe.

That said, some people quietly told me they would not be confident enough to approach someone wearing them even if they did spot them, for fear of the interaction being filmed and uploaded.

The glasses are designed to work as an extension of your phone. They use Bluetooth to sync with a handset via Meta's AI app. They are voice-activated, with open speakers in the arms funnelling sound into your ears. The result is a bit like wearing headphones without the addition of noise-cancelling features, so you can still hear the world around you.

My potentially cancellable opinion is that I found many of the glasses' features useful. Interestingly, none of them included the camera.

Listening to music and podcasts on the move without having earbuds stuffed into my ears felt safer. I felt more confident about avoiding the gamut of e-bike-riding phone thieves in central London without my phone physically in my hand.

And as someone with a pitiful sense of direction, I rely a lot on map apps. It was handy to have the directions spoken in my ears. The pay-off for this, however, was having to accept allowing the Meta AI app to know exactly where I was at all times. Meta is notorious for its hunger for personal data.

When I posted about using the Meta Ray-Bans on social media, I got a bit of a hard time. Less so when I showed them to people in my everyday life.

My hairdresser loved the idea of using them to record her clients' hair transformations. A builder I chatted to at the gym reckoned they would be useful on sites for recording what he was doing, either in the event of an accident or even to teach others new skills. My friend who runs said he would like to wear them on a jog.

Plenty of content creators are big fans. My son borrowed them to wash my car, and was proud of his film showing me how he delicately chipped away at a stubborn bit of bird poo without damaging the paintwork (I was pleased, and happy to take his word for it).

More broadly, smart glasses have been welcomed by the blind community. One user described them to the BBC as a "game-changer" because they can give audio descriptions of current locations and read out visible text like restaurant menu options. Earlier this year Meta donated 15,000 pairs to a charity for the blind in Ireland.

But still, anger over privacy has grown.

The glasses have a blinking white LED that switches on when the camera is active, but a whole industry has sprung up around finding technical workarounds to disable that light, some of which involve taking the glasses apart.

Meta says less than 0.1% of the frames it has sold worldwide have been physically tampered with. Exact sales figures are unknown, but Ray-Ban's parent company EssilorLuxottica has reported that it sold seven million last year.

Liz Hunter, a tech founder and parent who has set up a petition calling for urgent new regulation of smart glasses, is furious.

"They should never, ever have left the lab at Meta," she told me. "It's a real travesty of public trust, and of women's equality, and it's rolled back our privacy rights right before our very eyes."

Hunter thinks smart glasses should remain available for blind people, but not for the general population.

"We don't need them, we don't want them," she says.

A Polish developer has released an app called ZuckOff which uses Bluetooth to identify nearby smart glasses. It's been downloaded thousands of times, reports Wired magazine.

Ben Wood, from tech research firm CCS Insight, remembers first reading the phrase "pervert glasses" in the usually strait-laced Financial Times - a sign, he says, that it had prompted a "significant public backlash".

The furore has not deterred other companies from eyeing the market, however.

Samsung is reported to be working on a collaboration with the upmarket glasses brand Warby Parker. Google is also said to be working on a set. Snap, the firm behind Snapchat, has just launched Specs, which are retailing in the US for $2,195 (and £1,995 in the UK). Users can see data inside the glass, and snap their fingers to take a photo.

Snap founder Evan Spiegel says he thinks smart glasses will eventually replace phones, and he's not alone.

When Meta launched smart glasses in 2021, they were geared in part around what the user could see. The firm promised they would allow users to "easily record the world as you see it", and to "capture life's moments as they happen from a unique first-person perspective".

So Meta's latest announcement - glasses without a camera - is notable.

Janusz Swierczynski, a researcher at Oxford University's Saïd Business School, who is worried about smart glasses, says the release of a camera-free version is a "positive sign" that Meta seems to have listened to privacy concerns. "They're thinking about it and that they're responding," he says, though he thinks it's "not a perfect" response because the camera-enabled glasses are still on the market.

Others are less sure it represents a real shift.

"It's certainly not the end of cameras in glasses," says Wood, from CCS Insight. He thinks that smart glasses are largely about capturing information; the glasses collect as much data as they can from your surroundings and then use AI to tell you about it.

And glasses armed with a camera - trained on whatever you can see - are an "extremely good" source of that information.

"That is an invaluable data stream to an AI platform, which can then interpret that data and provide you with the best possible information related to it," Wood says. "So having the vision parts of it with the cameras is a key pillar for getting the best experience."

He imagines Meta has been working on the camera-free glasses for several years, and the current backlash over privacy provides "fantastic timing" for their release.

Indeed, Meta doesn't yet show any signs of slowing down its development of camera-enabled glasses. The company is bringing its third generation of the glasses to the UK next month. These can visually display data inside the specs' lenses. (As a live broadcast journalist who has talked openly about brain fog, I can see the appeal of glasses that can discreetly display a script).

Kate Winick, a tech analyst at the research firm Forrester, says it's not a step back from camera-enabled glasses but more of a "half step to the side, where they give users time to get comfortable with the technology… so that users themselves start to say, 'Oh, this would be so much more useful if it had a camera'."

And she says, paradoxically, the existence of camera-free glasses might help "take the heat" off people who wear camera-enabled glasses in public. "It's now clear that out in the market some glasses have cameras and some don't," she says. "You can't automatically get mad at everybody wearing Meta's glasses, because you may not know whether or not they have a camera."

And other companies are trying to address privacy concerns in different ways - without getting rid of the camera.

The Taiwanese firm HTC recently launched Vive Eagle glasses, which cost less than a quarter of Snap's.

Thomas Dexmier, a vice president at HTC Vive, says that if anyone near an Eagle specs wearer says "stop filming" or "stop recording", and it is picked up by one of the four microphones, the camera will deactivate.

And he adds that all recordings captured by the glasses are encrypted, and the firm itself cannot see them - though this also means HTC cannot flag harmful content.

"We acknowledge that there are some challenges, potentially becoming a real problem, especially for women," he said.

He said HTC Vive was working to make it as difficult as possible for the tech to be misused but said it was "too early to comment" on whether the firm would consider a version without cameras.

Ultimately, Wood thinks that camera-enabled glasses are "not going away".

He says the current moment reminds him of the 2000s, when some people said that mobile phone companies couldn't install cameras in their devices because of similar concerns over privacy. "There's an inevitability there," he says.

"We will have to find a societal norm, a framework for the use of these products."
