articles.title: Harry Potter play producer says cost of living made two-part show 'impossible'
articles.text:
A Harry Potter And The Cursed Child producer has said the rising cost of living made it "literally impossible" to retain the play's original format in two parts.

The production has been cut down to a single three-hour show and is set to re-open in the West End next month.

"The cost of living has gone up 30-40% since the pandemic, including running shows," producer Sonia Friedman said in comments reported by media at a launch event. "The only way we could continue to run it as a two-parter would be by charging an amount for the tickets that would be unaffordable and inaccessible."

The two-part play, a sequel to JK Rowling's books, premiered in the West End in 2016 and closed on 20 September.

The changes to the West End production follow the 2021 relaunch of the play as a single show on Broadway in New York City.

"The pandemic, the cost of living and the wars going on around the world accelerated that decision in New York, and that's where we are now with London," Friedman said.

"Of course we'll miss it but it was absolutely the right call and we've got a beautiful alternate version that we're very proud of."

Director John Tiffany said at the launch event that he and writer Jack Thorne - who also wrote acclaimed Netflix series Adolescence - had to be "dragged, kicking and screaming to make the one-parter" due to the success of their original script, the Times reported.

However, Tiffany said the new version meant "more people are going to get to see this show and not have to pay a fortune for it", according to The Stage.

The play takes place 19 years after the final book and follows Harry's son Albus Severus as he arrives at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.

The production has been seen by more than 14 million people around the world, including over 2.5 million in London.

The reimagined one-part production will retain some of its original cast, including David Ricardo-Pearce as Harry Potter, Thomas Aldridge as Ron Weasley and Naana Agyei Ampadu as Hermione Granger.

New actors have been cast in the roles of Albus Potter, Ginny Potter, Rose Granger-Weasley, Draco Malfoy and Scorpius Malfoy.

articles.title: Teen rocker Nene Royal becomes first Thai to win America's Got Talent
articles.text:
Nene Royal, a 16-year-old rocker, has been crowned the latest winner of America's Got Talent - making her the first ever Thai winner of the long-running talent show.

For the show's finals on Tuesday in California, Nene, whose real name is Rattikarn Amloy, performed a rendition of Seven Nation Army by American rock duo The White Stripes.

Her heavy metal performances trumped nine other finalists, including magician acts, canine performers and even a robot dance crew.

Many in Thailand are celebrating her win, with some saying they were proud that she had made it to "one of the biggest stages in the world". The Thai government has called her an "inspiration to anyone who dares to dream big".

Nene emerged as a clear fan favourite early in the competition, after a viral clip of her audition, in which she belted out Zombie by The Cranberries to a stunned panel of judges. The video has racked up 20 million views.

On Wednesday night, ahead of the results being announced, Nene took the stage with Linkin Park to perform The Emptiness Machine, a 2024 rock song by the American band.

Later that night she broke down in tears, kneeling on the ground as she was crowned the winner of the show's 21st season - which comes with a prize of $1m (£755,000).

"I'm very happy and emotional right now," she said, thanking everyone for supporting her.

The results show was also eagerly followed by her legion of fans in Thailand, who were unable to watch the live broadcast on the television network NBC.

Many in Thailand had to resort to a YouTube livestream instead - and were thrown into distress when the livestream was abruptly cut in the middle of the results announcements.

But moments later came sighs of relief and exclamations of joy, as word got around that Nene had secured her historic victory.

"History made!" one Thai social media user wrote on Facebook.

"Let the world write it down that this Thai kid is incredibly talented," wrote another.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul congratulated Nene Royal, saying in a statement that she had "brought honour to Thailand" and "instilled pride in the Thai people" with her win.

"What makes this win special is that Nene carried her Thai identity with confidence onto one of the world's biggest stages," the Thai government's public relations department said in another statement on Thursday.

"She showed that talent, hard work, and determination can come from anywhere, including a young girl from Phuket with a guitar and a big dream."

articles.title: Federal judge delays ruling on White House ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW
articles.text:
A federal judge has heard arguments between the Trump Administration and three news organisations over the decision to bar them from reporting inside White House grounds.

In a brief hearing in Washington on Wednesday, Judge Timothy Kelly weighed a request from CNN, Politico and MS NOW for a temporary restraining order to urgently restore White House passes to 78 reporters.

A lawyer for the media outlets said that the White House is falsely arguing that national security concerns justify the ban. A justice department lawyer said the president has the right to "exclude anyone he wants" from certain locations inside the White House.

The judge said he would come to a decision as soon as he could.

Last week, President Donald Trump barred CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news".

Their reporters had their passes confiscated and were denied access to the building, and the three outlets jointly launched legal action, calling the move unconstitutional.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico say they were stripped of their credentials because the President disliked their reporting.

Theodore Boutrous, representing the media outlets, argued on Wednesday that the White House had manufactured a national security argument as a way to retaliate against news organisations perceived as critical of Trump.

"They're literally arguing that reporters shouldn't scrutinise national security issues and decisions by the government," he said.

He noted that Trump never cited national security when he ordered the ban in a Truth Social post last Friday. The justification was added later on, he told the judge.

Michael Velchik, a lawyer for the US Department of Justice, opened his argument in court by asserting that "access to the White House is a privilege, not a right".

He claimed that the news organisations had published information that could harm national security, which Boutrous disputed.

"The viewpoint discrimination is probably the clearest case in history. I mean, the president said, 'I don't like what you're publishing. I'm taking away your press pass based on that,'" he told the hearing.

"They are using national security as this talisman — these magic words," Boutrous said. "It is just a pretextual, post hoc effort to justify just a blatant violation of due process."

He asked the judge to rule quickly, due to "urgent matters" that require news coverage, including the Iran war, the UN General Assembly taking place in New York City, Chinese President Xi Jinping's US visit, and the debate over AI regulation.

In court filings ahead of Wednesday's hearing, the justice department filed a series of "reporting incidents" they said justified the ban.

The filing cites a number of stories about construction at the White House - including about a security bunker and the building of a new ballroom, as well as a report on an internal information leak investigation.

The three media organisations have argued that the ban breaches their rights under the First Amendment, which forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press.

In a joint statement confirming legal action against the government, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting.

"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

Forty-nine media organisations - including CBS News, The New York Times and Fox News - filed a legal brief in support of the lawsuit against the White House.

Major TV networks have withdrawn from a media-sharing arrangement of video and images of the president, known as the pool, in protest over the ban.

Shortly after, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, which operates a 24/7 feed of clips of the president.

articles.title: Louise Kennedy: Author whose character was played by Gillian Anderson unfazed by 'second book syndrome'
articles.text:
When your award-winning debut novel is adapted into a Bafta-nominated TV series expectations run high for what might come next.

But Louise Kennedy, the author of Trespasses, seems unfazed with the daunting notion of what is often called second book syndrome.

Maybe it's her late entrance to the literary world, working in busy kitchens as a chef for decades or dealing with a cancer diagnosis that helps Kennedy cope with pressure.

She says she "could very easily never have written a word" and continued her career as a chef.

"I'm sure my life wouldn't have been thoroughly miserable," she adds with a half smile.

But in 2014, aged 47, a friend asked her to join a writing group.

"I had never written in my life. I had no ambition to write. It never entered my head."

At first it was short stories, then came Trespasses in 2022.

Set during the Troubles in Northern Ireland it was a story of cross-community forbidden love between a young Catholic teacher and a married Protestant barrister.

Kennedy's second novel is Stations, currently being serialised on BBC Radio 4, the reader meets Róisín and Red, following their friendship from rural Ireland to London, full of teenage angst, fragile friendships and the romance of escape.

"I knew that there were going to be readers for Stations, but I could only write the book that I wanted to write," she tells BBC News.

Their story starts in County Kildare in 1982 and follows them for the next 25 years as Róisín follows Red to London.

Kennedy describes her relationship with Róisín, as "unfinished business" as the lead character is the same unsympathetic teenager from her 2021 collections of short stories The End of the World is a Cul-de-sac.

Kennedy goes to great pains to declare that Róisín isn't her and she's not Róisín, "but there are similarities".

Kennedy and her family left Northern Ireland when she was 12 in the 1970s and relocated to the Republic of Ireland where she found herself an outsider in a small, rural village.

"I was a very unpopular, awkward teenager but I'm a good mimic. I thought that all my problems in my new school would be solved if I spoke like everybody else. And I was able to change my accent over a weekend."

This accent change is also something Kennedy gifts to Róisín and the book pokes at the very pronunciation of her name, "Rawsheen" in the north, but "Rowsheen" in the south.

The decision to sacrifice her Belfast accent is something she regrets.

However, she explains that when she is writing her early life experiences resurface.

"When I speak, I sound like a free stater, but the voice in my head is really northern."

The parallels don't end there, as Kennedy, similar to the characters in Stations, also emigrated to England in the 1980s. However, Kennedy moved for economic reasons.

"Most of us went to London because you didn't have to get a visa. It was cheap and there was a huge network of people there.

"You always knew people, and there were always leads for getting a place in a squat or some horrible flat somewhere."

There are about 500,000 Irish-born people living in England today.

Since the 1930s, England has been the major focus for Irish migration, with big waves during the 1940s to the 1950s and the Irish recession of the 1980s.

However, Kennedy was keenly aware of the generation ahead of her who emigrated in the 1940s and 50s.

The women ending up in domestic roles or nursing and the men mostly labouring across building sites unable to settle.

She says "we weren't so different".

"We were better educated, but we had great expectations and great hopes for ourselves."

Last year, Trespasses was turned into a Channel 4 drama, starring Gillian Anderson and Lola Petticrew giving the story a "much longer and bigger life" than Kennedy ever anticipated.

So has Kennedy thought about where her new novel could go and who she would cast?

The short answer is no.

Whilst the book has been auctioned for TV and film adaptation rights, Kennedy is putting no names in the mix.

"I kind of sat back a lot with that because I just thought it wouldn't be helpful for me to be asking loads of questions."

However, with a sly smile Kennedy confesses that her granny "would have been absolutely tickled pink to think of Gillian Anderson playing her".

In Trespasses, Anderson plays the character Gina, who has alcoholism and is the broken mother of Cushla, based on a version of Kennedy's grandmother.

"Even as a scruffy Gillian Anderson, she'd have been thrilled."

In 2019, Kennedy was diagnosed with melanoma skin cancer, which, over the following years progressed to further discoveries and a stage 4 diagnosis.

She googled everything - apart from her prognosis.

"I never asked. I never said 'how long have I got if these drugs don't work'," she says.

The drugs were successful and after eight months the cancer was gone but there are ongoing health challenges as a result.

She has previously praised Trespasses for enabling her to "largely ignore all the health stuff, external" as the writing of it Kennedy told The Times “got her through the first melanoma diagnosis", and its publication, sustained her through its return.

It's then not surprising that the acknowledgement in her new novel pays homage to the medical team who continue to look after her and "the legend who figured out how to use Chinese hamster ovary cells against melanoma".

"I owe you my life."

But Louise Kennedy, the author of Trespasses, seems unfazed with the daunting notion of what is often called second book syndrome. Maybe it's her late entrance to the literary world,...

articles.title: Michael Kiwanuka: Singer reveals he is recovering from a stroke
articles.text:
Award-winning singer-songwriter Michael Kiwanuka has revealed he has suffered a stroke and faces a "long, tough journey ahead" to recover.

The 39-year-old from London, who won the Mercury Prize in 2020 and has been nominated for five Brit Awards, said in an Instagram post that the stroke occurred "a few months ago" and was caused "by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure".

He added that "the brain injury I suffered was quite severe so there's a lot of rehab to be done", but told fans he will "look forward to seeing you all soon".

Kiwanuka simultaneously announced the release of his fifth album, titled Fudge, which was recorded before the stroke.

"I'm very happy to be announcing to you my new album Fudge," his message said.

"I'm especially happy because the last few months I've been battling some health problems which would heavily hinder and get in the way of me making music for the foreseeable future. A few months ago I suffered a stroke brought on by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure.

"It's a long journey recovering from a stroke, which is why I missed some gigs recently out in the US, but I look forward to seeing you all soon.

"I'm not sure when I'll be able to be back out on the road or what that will look like, the brain injury I suffered was quite severe so there's a lot of rehab to be done, it's a long, tough journey ahead but I'm fighting to get better.

"It has been a difficult few months I must say but it feels like I'm on my way there now."

He thanked "all the incredible NHS staff and every single medical professional who has helped care for me and continue to help and encourage me in my recovery", and his friends and family for their support.

"This has definitely been one of the toughest challenges I've faced and I'll be happy to be on the other side of it when the time comes. Until then I wish you all well and look forward to seeing you further down the road."

Fans and fellow artists sent well wishes, with BBC Radio 6 Music presenter Lauren Laverne replying: "So sorry to read this, Michael. What a time you must have had. Really glad you have good care and wishing you a full recovery asap. One day at a time. Xx."

US singer Miguel wrote: "Man, take your time healing, you are needed brother."

Radiohead guitarist Ed O'Brien posted: "Sending love to you Michael."

articles.title: Nigella Lawson is 'brilliant addition' to The Great British Bake Off, TV critics say
articles.text:
TV critics have described Nigella Lawson as the "icing on the cake" of The Great British Bake Off, after the show returned for a new series on Tuesday.

Lawson has replaced Dame Prue Leith, who announced she was leaving earlier this year after nearly a decade in the programme's famous tent.

The Telegraph said Lawson gives the Channel 4 series a "new lease of life", while Digital Spy agreed she was a "brilliant addition" to the line-up.

But the Independent was cooler on the launch episode as a whole, saying the show "wastes Nigella's prodigious charms and misses a chance for a true revamp".

The return of Bake Off saw Lawson join fellow judge Paul Hollywood, who has appeared on the programme since its launch in 2010, and presenters Alison Hammond and Noel Fielding.

Former Bake Off winner Giuseppe Dell'Anno told BBC Radio 4's Today that Lawson "did produce a step change" to the show and was a "nice fit with the ethos of the programme".

"She was doing her best by capturing the vibes of a cake, the feelings, what it makes you think of, which was very nicely balanced by Paul being very technical and scrutinising," he said.

"I think, however, that she will get better over time, because my gut feeling yesterday was that she was still in new territory."

In a five-star review, the Guardian's Lucy Mangan said, external Lawson "moves through Bake Off dispensing words of wisdom, generous praise and gentle criticism".

She added that Lawson is "just as confident as Leith but a much quieter, more soothing presence that works perfectly with Alison Hammond's ebullience and Paul Hollywood's teacher-ish vibe".

The Telegraph's Anita Singh also awarded, external five stars, remarking that "Bake Off and Nigella are a match made in heaven".

"She brings glamour, intelligence and poise. And, of course, a hefty dollop of innuendo," Singh said.

"Lawson is supportive in her judging but not afraid to tell the bakers where they can improve. She gives helpful advice."

The launch episode was described as "one of the most disastrous openers ever" by Metro's Adam Miller, external - but luckily he was only referring to the cakes.

"When Bake Off should be crumbling after 17 seasons, Nigella Lawson is making Channel 4's crown jewel fresher than ever," he said.

"It's clear to see she is the lifeline Bake Off needed to ensure it could easily have another decade or more in it yet."

When Lawson was faced with innuendo-laden comments from contestants or co-stars, she often "wisely said nothing", noted the Daily Mail's Jan Moir., external

"Ultimately this was a tremendous debut performance from the new mistress of meringue, showing a side of Nigella we have not seen before: quirky, commanding, funny – but also humane," she concluded.

Ben Dowell of the Times observed, external: "Bake Off has always been one of TV's more beguiling offerings with a comforting romance about it.

"It's not perfect. Hammond is ebullience and warmth personified but her co-presenter, the erstwhile Mighty Boosh comedian Fielding, still looks a bit lost, as if he has wandered in from the wrong set.

"But with Nigella the show is definitely in safe hands. Bake Off has found a new star."

articles.title: Dolly Parton's manager accuses nephew who announced her death of threats and intimidation
articles.text:
Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's legacy and business interests.

The accusations against Bryan Seaver, who was Parton's head of security and was handpicked to announce her death last month, have been made public in US legal documents filed this week.

The company that manages Parton's businesses and properties, She's Alive, is seeking a temporary civil restraining order against him.

In court filings, She's Alive alleged that Seaver mounted "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", claiming he said he would ruin her empire if the estate did not pay him. He has denied the claims.

In a statement to TMZ, external, he said that text messages and emails quoted in the court application had been taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people.

"Nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by," he said.

"A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."

Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns a company that provided the singer's security detail for the last 20 years of her life.

Last week, he was fired by She's Alive as head of security for her properties.

In a statement at the time, Seaver and his company said the dismissal was "unexpected" and "unexplained".

They added: "We refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much."

The request for a restraining order was filed in Nashville on Tuesday by She's Alive, which is run by Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell.

The court documents quoted a series of exchanges in which someone, identified by the estate as Seaver, threatened to destroy Parton's brand.

In one, he's alleged to have said he would become "the hand of retribution for my entire family", according to the court documents.

Another said: "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or [expletive] pay me."

The papers also claimed that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees.

In an exchange with one of Parton's lawyers, he allegedly described himself as a "killer" and said that on the day his aunt died, he had sold $27m (£20m) in arms and ammunition to the Haitian police.

"All I do is warfare... Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do," he was accused of saying, according to a copy of an email attached to the complaint.

In his statement published on TMZ, Seaver said: "I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer."

But he denied making threats and said he had been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend".

The messages have resulted in some employees and lawyers for Parton's trusts and estates resigning, according to the court documents.

She's Alive has also had to hire private security for its employees, including at their homes, the filing states.

The BBC has contacted Seaver and She's Alive for further comment.

Previously, Seaver was known to the public for announcing his aunt's death in a video posted to her Instagram account on 25 August.

Speaking in front of a black background, he was sombre and reflective as he introduced himself and shared the unexpected news.

"This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," he said in the video.

Seaver added that he had followed in his father Larry's footsteps in becoming Parton's head of security, a post he held for more than 20 years.

Nozell started working for Parton in 2004, first as a tour consultant and later as her manager.

In the 2019 Netflix film, Dolly Parton: Here I Am, he said his job was to transform her from a "heritage act" into a "superstar", and he took responsibility for reviving her international touring career.

In a statement last month, he said the singer had "worked up until the day she died" on multiple projects, and envisioned a legacy that continued long beyond her death.

"She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy," he said in the statement.

"Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come."

The estate now faces a public tug of war over that legacy.

articles.title: Petition for Sir Tom Jones to return to The Voice backed by Will.i.am
articles.text:
Will.i.am has endorsed a petition to have Sir Tom Jones reinstated on ITV's The Voice.

Sir Tom told his social media followers earlier this month that the broadcaster had "fired" him as a judge on the show.

The 86-year-old singer from Treforest, Rhondda Cynon Taf, has appeared as an on-off coach on the singing competition since it premiered in 2012.

Superfan Aaron Howlett, 50, from Kingston-upon-Hull, started the petition which has received more than 63,000 signatures from around the world.

ITV thanked Sir Tom for all of his years on The Voice and the "countless incredible and unforgettable moments" he gave the show.

Speaking on BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Wednesday, Howlett said he had been a fan of Sir Tom for four decades.

"Sir Tom is one of the last living legends," he said. "His voice resonates with so many people, young and old."

"If he stopped singing and performing, then he wouldn't be Sir Tom anymore," continued Howlett.

"I think singing is Tom. He resonates from the inside and he becomes alive on stage."

Howlett referenced a recent show Jones performed in Milwaukee, USA, where he "was given a standing ovation at 86".

"He rocked the crowd. He had the crowd in the palm of his hand. He still does it on the television, and he's the reason that most people watch The Voice," he said.

US rapper and songwriter Will.i.am, who has also appeared as a coach on The Voice alongside Sir Tom, collaborated on a Change.org Instagram post on 15 September which shared Howlett's petition.

Howlett said he was "overwhelmed" by the response as, when he started it, he was unsure if "anybody [was] going to follow".

Fans from across the world have commented on the online petition, including Alison, from Peterborough, who wrote: "I, like so many people, watch The Voice because of Sir Tom and will stop watching if he's not on it."

Carmela, from Montreal in Canada, said: "My mom passed away three years ago. On her death bed she had to watch Tom Jones on TV and on YouTube. Us Canadians love him. My mom and I went to see him in concert three times when he came to visit my city."

An ITV spokesperson said: "ITV would like to thank Sir Tom Jones for all his years on The Voice UK, and the countless incredible and unforgettable moments he gave the show.

"He has brought joy to audiences, and to every singer who performed for him and with him."

articles.title: Netherlands to return to Eurovision after 2026 boycott
articles.text:
The Netherlands will return to the Eurovision Song Contest next year despite a boycott by the broadcaster that was previously in charge of the country's participation.

Dutch network Avrotros withdrew in 2026 and said it would also not take part in 2027 because the competition could "no longer be considered neutral" given divisions over Israel's involvement and the Gaza war.

The NPO, which oversees public broadcasting in the country, has now stepped in, saying coverage of the contest will be provided by broadcasting organisation NOS, while an independent panel will select the Dutch participant.

Jurre Bosman, NPO's director of media, said: "It is important that, as a public broadcaster, we remain part of this unifying European event at this moment in particular."

Israel's participation in the contest has become highly controversial, and five countries, including the Netherlands, boycotted this year's event.

Eurovision organiser the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) has subsequently announced a number of changes, including to exclude any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.

That means that, although Israel can still compete, the EBU would ask another country to host if it won.

The EBU has also proposed changes to to the voting, saying politically motivated voting has become "persistent" and is widely seen as "deeply worrying".

However, Avrotros said those changes did "not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored".

In a statement on Wednesday, the NPO said the EBU has "taken significant steps regarding the rules" of the contest, and that the Netherlands will return.

Acknowledging that the contest provokes "mixed feelings" in the Netherlands, the NPO said it had "explicitly asked the EBU to once again make the unifying character of the festival an important part of the event".

The NPO also said the Dutch entrant would be chosen by "an independent team of experts" who would "carefully guide the process surrounding the act".

Eurovision director Martin Green said in a statement: "We are delighted to welcome the Netherlands back to the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027.

"We value the constructive conversations we have had with NPO and look forward to working together to reinforce the Contest as a place that truly reflects the spirit of 'United By Music'."

Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all pulled out of the 2026 contest in addition to the Netherlands.

The 2027 contest will take place on 14 May in Burgas, after Bulgarian singer Dara won this year's contest with Bangaranga.

articles.title: Angry Anderson, who soundtracked Kylie Monigue's wedding in Neighbours scene, dies aged 79
articles.text:
Rock star Angry Anderson, whose music famously soundtracked the wedding of Kylie Minogue and Jason Donovan's characters in Australian TV soap Neighbours, has died at the age of 79.

The musician, whose real name was Gary Anderson, rose to fame as the frontman of Rose Tattoo, one of Australia's most revered rock bands, from 1976.

His solo song Suddenly became a global hit after it was played during the wedding of Minogue and Donovan's characters Scott and Charlene in Neighbours. The episode was watched by 20 million people in the UK in 1988.

Anderson said Minogue had been "adamant" that the track was used for the scene, and he later declared that Suddenly was the best song he had ever written.

Paying tribute to Anderson on Instagram, Donovan said: "Legend! What a great guy.

"Another great Australian. Thank you Angry for all the wonderful music and memories. Condolences to all friends and family."

Before his death, Anderson had a cardiac arrest while on Rose Tattoo's farewell tour in Europe last month.

He was treated in hospital before going home to Australia, and the band cancelled nine live dates.

A joint statement, external from Anderson's family and Rose Tattoo remembered him as a "devoted father, and much-loved bandmate".

"His loss will be deeply felt by all those who knew and loved him both here in Australia and overseas," it said.

"We thank everyone for their prayers and messages of love and continued support."

articles.title: George Bush, murder and nautical infidelity: the Chicks’ 20 greatest songs – ranked!
articles.text:
20. If I Fall You’re Going Down With Me (2001)

One of eight singles released from the album Fly. Amazement at the sheer number should be matched by astonishment at their consistency. If I Fall … is just great. Organ-driven rock lent a Nashville twang by the fiddle, it barrels along, rich with the confidence of a band who know they can’t put a foot wrong.

19. Tights on My Boat (2020)

You don’t want for dirt dished about Natalie Maines’ divorce on Gaslighter, the band’s eighth album, but this accusation of nautical infidelity stands out. It’s ferociously angry and very funny – plus its understated, live-in the-studio sound only compounds the sense that you’re eavesdropping on tea being spilled among friends.

18. You Were Mine (1998)

A great country weeper in its own right, You Were Mine is also part of the Chicks’ origin story. It was written by the sisters Emily Strayer and Martie Maguire about their parents’ divorce; they then invited Maines, the daughter of the producer Lloyd Maines, to sing on the demo, rather than the then Chicks vocalist Laura Lynch. A lineup change and vast success ensued.

17. The Long Way Around (2006)

The chief theme of the Taking the Long Way album – being celebrated soon with a 20th anniversary reissue and tour – was the Chicks’ war of words with President George W Bush and Nashville conservatives. The musically sweet-toned opening track suggests that attitude was par for the course – of a piece with a longstanding disinclination to “kiss all the asses” and “do it like everybody else”.

16. Julianna Calm Down (2020)

Over a soft organ backing and something approaching a dancefloor pulse, the Chicks offer hard-won advice to the recently dumped: “Put on your best shoes and strut the fuck around like you’ve got nothing to lose.” Its slow build to a euphoric climax – elevated by Maguire’s fiddle – is great.

15. Ready to Run (1999)

You could suggest the Celtic motifs on Ready to Run are an acknowledgment of Irish folk’s seminal influence on country; equally, they may have something to do with the Corrs’ late-90s success. Either way, Ready to Run’s breezy mood carries a witty lyric that offers a middle finger to marriage and commitment.

14. Texas Man (2020)

Marooned in California post-divorce, Maines pines for the more rough-hewn gents of her home county. But the beauty of Texas Man is really about the music’s experimental bent: a tight, close-miked, new-wave-leaning sound replete with fuzzed-out guitar that’s completely unlike anything the Chicks had released before, but still somehow sounds like them.

13. Cold Day in July (1999)

Five minutes of inconsolable misery. “The moon is full, and my arms are empty / All night long, I’ve pleaded and cried,” it opens, with Maines’ voice at its most angst-ridden. The guitar-driven arrangement is simple, but spot-on: it doesn’t need anything more to work its sob-inducing magic.

12. Sin Wagon (1999)

In the early 80s, there was talk of a subgenre called cowpunk. It never crossed over into the mainstream, but the title perfectly fits Sin Wagon, named after a line in Grease. A thrilling blend of speedy bluegrass with raw, growling energy, its lyrics are home to a splendid celebration of “mattress dancin”.

11. Sleep at Night (2020)

There’s a pleasing circularity about Sleep at Night, which bears the distinct influence of the noted Chicks fan Taylor Swift; you can almost hear her delivering the line: “My husband’s girlfriend’s husband just called me up – how messed up is that?” An extra point for the slapping rhythm track, the perfect accompaniment to the punches landed in the lyrics.

10. Easy Silence (2006)

The negative image of Taking the Long Way’s two-fisted lead single Not Ready to Make Nice, Easy Silence details the downside of being the centre of a media storm. It sounds utterly, affectingly weary – “everyone is running” it notes, before evincing a longing to “keep the world at bay”.

9. There’s Your Trouble (1998)

The Chicks’ biggest UK chart hit offers the perfect example of why their fourth album, Wide Open Spaces, catapulted the former bluegrass/western-swing combo to superstardom: beautifully turned songwriting, a fresh pop sheen that didn’t overwhelm their audible country bona fides, impressively tough and salty lyrics and – in their new vocalist Maines – the ideal voice to deliver them.

8. Landslide (2002)

This version of the Stevie Nicks song is bold – the original is a classic – and ahead of the curve, arriving years before Fleetwood Mac became a hip name for leftfield musicians to drop. Stripped down to country basics, in keeping with the rest of the album Home, the song shines, highlighting the trio’s impeccable harmonies.

7. Long Time Gone (2002)

The back-to-the-land saga of Darrell Scott’s Long Time Gone comes complete with a critique of modern Nashville – “they got money, but they don’t have Cash” – and the Chicks’ version is suitably old-fashioned, with no drums and a distinct bluegrass influence about the banjo and fiddle. The lyrics are biting, but it still sounds like a party.

6. Gaslighter (2020)

The title track of the first Chicks album in 14 years pulled no punches. Its subject, Natalie Maines’ ex-husband Adrian Pasdar, had reportedly been concerned that the group’s unreleased material would violate a confidentiality clause in their prenuptial agreement. Gaslighter was released after the couple finalised their divorce, but it is almost unsettlingly brutal in its frankness – and insanely catchy.

5. Wide Open Spaces (1998)

Wide Open Spaces started life as a student’s poem about returning to Texas from university in Montana and ended up a kind of Stetson-clad She’s Leaving Home. A huge hit – and the kind of Chicks song that one suspects sunk in deep with the young Swift.

4. Travelin’ Soldier (2002)

This is destined to be remembered as the track Maines was introducing in London when she criticised Bush, but the ensuing furore shouldn’t overshadow how fantastic Travelin’ Soldier is. Stark and moving, never mawkish, it isn’t a protest song so much as a heartbreaking story entwined with the Vietnam war.

3. Cowboy Take Me Away (1999)

A song based on the slogan of a US advert – for Calgon bath and beauty products! – should be a novelty. Cowboy Take Me Away is anything but. Instead, it’s a wistful paean to escape, lent a tear-jerking quality by the sense said escape may never happen. Balanced between uplift and melancholy, the music fits perfectly.

2. Not Ready to Make Nice (2006)

The Chicks’ best-known musical response to the Bush incident is a thing of snarling, screw-the-lot-of-you wonder: “It’s too late to make it right / I probably wouldn’t if I could.” The ensuing album slightly belaboured the point, but as a short, sharp burst of bitterness and bile, Not Ready to Make Nice is a triumph.

1. Goodbye Earl (1999)

Long before controversy engulfed their career, the Chicks were entirely capable of causing it. Twenty country stations refused to play Goodbye Earl, apparently horrified by the lyric: high school friends Mary-Anne and Wanda successfully plot to murder Wanda’s abusive husband after he breaches a restraining order and leaves her in intensive care. It still sold a million copies – deservedly so. The chorus is a singalong monster, the lyric is gripping and superbly written and the Chicks’ reading of it is perfect. The vocals switch from cold rage to gleeful celebration over music that is taut and explosive. Tongues firmly in cheek, they stuck a cover of Stand By Your Man on the B-side.

articles.title: ‘My first screen kiss was in a cowshed!’ Lesley Manville on her greatest roles – and why sex scenes for over-50s are booming
articles.text:
It is high summer and, while Lesley Manville may be suffering a bit with hay fever and the heat (“I’m so white, all I do is burn”), she doesn’t do wilting. Soon to head outside to tend to the ailing garden of her London home, she is enjoying a rare period of rest after six almost unbroken months of Oedipus on Broadway and then Les Liaisons Dangereuses at the National. She keeps, incidentally, the Tony she won for playing Jocasta in Oedipus on a shelf by the computer, “next to its friend, Larry Olivier” – an Olivier awarded for the same role.

“You don’t go into a job thinking about awards,” she says, before grinning conspiratorially. “Listen, you don’t say to an Olympian, ‘Oh, is it OK that you didn’t win?’ Yes, you like to win!”

Manville has done a fair bit of winning recently, and not before time. The last 15 years have seen her graduate from widely respected actor to garlanded star: since 2011 there has been that Tony, two Oliviers, an Oscar nomination for Paul Thomas Anderson’s Phantom Thread, Emmy and Golden Globe nominations and seven Bafta nominations. Her cinematic collaborators have included not only PTA but Luca Guadagnino, Alfonso Cuarón and Joel Coen. This relatively late blooming has come as a relief.

“I’m so glad I was never flavour of the month,” she says, “because it’s so hard to maintain. No one went to LA for pilot season when I was young – we were just interested in doing the work. But you’re right, there has been a shift. Winning the Olivier for Ibsen’s Ghosts in 2014 took me somewhere else, theatre-wise. An Oscar nomination makes a difference. A whole sequence of high-profile television, not least The Crown, which obviously wasn’t all about Princess Margaret but boy did Peter Morgan write me two astonishing episodes. Mrs Harris Goes to Paris brought me to a new audience, and Mum is the thing I still get stopped about most.”

These are just some of the most recent projects from an amazing body of work, one of which Manville – whose combination of wry wit, warm intelligence and stern savvy keeps me on my toes throughout our conversation – is rightly proud. Marble Hall Murders, her new TV series, starting on BBC One this week, completes Anthony Horowitz’s trilogy of ingenious Susan Ryeland mysteries. It may be one of her lighter pieces, but it’s no less satisfying for that.

Manville was willingly cajoled into returning as publisher-cum-crimebuster Ryeland by Horowitz, who offered to write a third book if she’d do a third series. Susan is back being single, back in London and back in publishing – albeit reluctantly – when a young writer proposes to conclude the bestselling saga of fictional detective Atticus Pünd. As before, many of the cast take dual roles as fact and fiction intertwine, and Pünd’s investigation into the murder of a publicly beloved, privately monstrous children’s author in Corfu is reflected by events in Susan’s world, where her sparring partners include Mark Bonnar and Rupert Penry Jones. If it is indeed the end, Manville will miss Susan immensely.

“She feels closer to me than a lot of other parts I’ve played. I like to think I don’t conform to a received notion of how one should be when one reaches a certain age. I love the fact that she wears these fabulous clothes, drives an open-top red sports car – I used to drive an MG in my 20s, although it broke down all the time – and doesn’t put up with any shit. Like her, I’m very clear about who I am. I’ve found myself at this point in my life. And although I’m absolutely terrible at guessing whodunnit, I’ve caught out a few boyfriends in the past, so my detective work hasn’t been all bad.”

Manville, now 70, grew up on a council estate in Hove, a seaside town in East Sussex, one of three daughters of lifelong Labour supporters. “Those principles stay with you. My early influences were very leftwing, working at the Royal Court with actors and playwrights who felt the same way.” These included Andrea Dunbar and Caryl Churchill. “I really want the Labour party to be everything it could be, and under Andy Burnham, we might have a glimmer of hope that happens. I’ve got a lot of time for him.”

Manville was a gifted performer from a young age, albeit not in the art form she would go on to conquer. “I had a really good, classically trained voice when I was young,” she says. “I could have been an opera singer, but something about it felt formal and stiff, so my 15-year-old brain went, ‘OK, I’ll go and do musicals.’”

Thanks to a council grant she commuted daily to London’s Italia Conti stage school, and, after O-levels, studied dance, singing and drama. “From my first job in a musical when I was 16 until I was 22, I did every job I was offered. I was a presenter. I did two pantomimes, a musical, a telly play, everything, but I never thought about playing characters. I just played me. Meeting Mike Leigh was the lightbulb moment, not just because he told me I was good but because I played someone a million miles from me. And I thought, ‘This is what I want to do.’”

That was in 1979, and Manville has now worked with Leigh more than any other actor, their eight films together producing what were, for years, her defining screen roles. Lonely daytime drinker Mary in Another Year, and the nervy, vulnerable breadwinner Penny in All or Nothing, in particular, condensed so much of what makes her great: the precision of characterisation, the deep dredging of despair, the dogged resilience. She still values Leigh’s opinion more than almost anyone else’s.

She even turned down an offer to join Arlene Phillips’ dancing troupe Hot Gossip. When I suggest she could resurrect her dancing on Strictly, she gently corrects me, explaining that she never really let it die. I should have guessed from her enviably upright deportment. “I’ve spent every night of the last three months dancing with professionals in Les Liaisons Dangereuses,” she says. “It felt like an extreme sport and it’s been wonderful!”

She pauses before taking a brief, impassioned detour. “Thank God, just because we’re over 50, we don’t have to have walking sticks – or not be thought of as sexual any more. We are! Oedipus and Les Liaisons were both highly sexualised pieces of theatre and I love that. Anyway, if I’d been asked to do Strictly 15 years ago, I might have said yes. Now, I’m not available much.”

She has been busy ever since her breakthrough TV role back in 1975, in ITV’s then new daytime soap Emmerdale Farm. “My first screen kiss was in a cowshed!” she says, hooting with laughter. “My character was younger and adored an older man. It was more affectionate than passionate. I’ve been kissed in more glamorous locations since.”

As with so many actors, soap opera gave her an “amazing grounding” in the technique and discipline of screen acting. “But I knew it was time to go. I remember a lot of the cast saying, ‘Oh, you shouldn’t leave. It’s great money. You’ve got security.’ I just thought, ‘I know, I hear you, I’ve learned a lot, it’s been amazing. But I’m off.’”

At times, her work rate frankly boggles the mind. For 10 weeks in 2018, for instance, she spent her days filming the costume drama Harlots in Watford and her evenings on the West End stage for Long Day’s Journey into Night. Where did this all come from?

“I just want to keep going. You’re either that person or you’re not. I’m very good at looking after myself. Just crack on with it is very much my philosophy and not a lot fazes me. If there was an Olympic event for multitasking, I’d win! When I was a single mum, I went back to work because I had to.” Gary Oldman, her first husband, left her, and the UK, three months after their son Alfie was born in 1989. “When I had too much to do, a play to learn and a baby who needed feeding and bathing and stories, I allocated my time much better.”

Alfie is now a father of three and a cameraman who has worked on projects with both his parents. “My friend Alan Rickman was on Harry Potter,” Manville remembers, “and he said, ‘Alfie, I’ll get you through the door [as a runner], but the rest is up to you,’ which was exactly right. Now if I see Alfie at work I’ll think, ‘What are you doing here?’ What a privilege. And he likes me. I like him. So it’s a win-win.”

Manville’s work ethic and eye for quality endure: days after we speak, it is announced that she will star with Anna Maxwell Martin in a new production of the American tragicomedy August: Osage County, and she is currently filming a new Prime series called Escorted, playing a Manhattan nightclub singer opposite Brett Goldstein as her son. There will be no slowing down for this formidable performer.

“I’ve got as much energy as all of those dancers I’ve just finished working with,” she says matter-of-factly. “I really am a bit like Susan Ryeland. I couldn’t give a fuck how old I am!”
